subject: hydra
pitch:
Category: Monster.
Subject: five-headed hydra.
Style: God of War.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module for a five-headed hydra in a God of War aesthetic—dark, scarred, armored, with glowing runes and ember-like accents—and sketching out the overall scale and body proportions before building it out.

Now I'm working out the skeleton structure: a root hip joint, a spine chain curving up toward the chest, four thick legs, a curling tail, and five separate neck chains branching from the shoulders, each ending in its own jaw-equipped head, all positioned along the forward z-axis.

Simplifying the bone setup further, I'll just keep one body sweep from rump to chest using the spine chain and hips joint together, avoiding extra complexity since smooth skinning works fine by default.

Plotting tail points curving down and back from the hips, then moving to leg placement -- positioning front legs with shoulders and feet coordinates, planning limb bends so the elbows angle backward for a sprawled, lizard-like stance.

For the hind legs I'll go digitigrade with three segments—thigh, shin, and foot with a sole—using a limb function to compute joint positions with bend hints, checking the total segment length reaches the foot target comfortably. I'm naming the joints hip, knee, ankle, and toe for each hind leg chain.

I'll determine left/right labeling based on sign of the side coordinate, then plan paw assemblies: each foot gets an ellipsoid base plus three forward-angled toe capsules tipped with claw spikes, positioned relative to the foot tip and built through a helper paw function.

Now for the five necks, I'm planning their fan-like splay from the chest's shoulder hump, each following an S-curved Catmull path up and outward to varied head heights, parented to the chest joint, with chains of five joints each plus head and jaw segments.

Then I'll add a jaw joint parented to the head, and think through orientation: the neck's final tangent should curve forward so the head faces mostly forward with the snout pointing slightly down. I'll use the "words" form (forward/up/etc.) for placing head geometry safely relative to the frame, since that avoids axis confusion compared to raw directional vectors.

Note that local x maps to -s*w since positive x is model-right which is world negative X, so I need to flip sign by side. Now I'm designing the hydra's neck fan, placing head positions by index with the center head tallest and outer heads lower and wider, computing their forward-ish endpoint coordinates.

Working out the neck bases along the chest top and sketching the S-curve path from base to head endpoint for each neck.

Still computing bezier points...

The belly sector orientation on the vertical neck is ambiguous since the neck curves forward — I'll instead countershade based on surface normal direction, making the front-facing concave side paler and the top darker, rather than relying on a fixed clock angle.

For dorsal ridge plates, I'm trusting the transported frame to keep angle 0 consistently pointing to the outer/back side of the tube as it rises and curves, so the spines stay aligned along the true back of the neck.

Now I'm thinking through head design—draugr/dragon-like with scars, horns, bone armor plating, and glowing ember eyes. I'll build the skull as a lofted shape with stations defining width and height along the snout axis.

Simplifying with frustumBox pieces for the upper snout and lower jaw, with widths running along world X for the default roll orientation, plus a sphere-based cranium scaled per head size.

I'm setting up a helper function that orients each head part along the bone's direction axis, so scale maps to width, length-along-bone, and depth consistently for every piece.

Now I'm working out the skull and snout placement along the neck-to-head axis using frustum boxes, sizing the head width relative to neck radius so heads read as proportionally larger than the necks feeding into them.

Adding brow ridges with angled capsules over the eyes, then building the eyes themselves with glowing ember-orange sphere parts and slit pupils for that predatory look.

Decals risk projection errors if not near surface, so I'll go simpler: build the eye as a glowing orange ellipsoid bulging from the socket, with a thin dark ellipsoid slit positioned slightly further out for the pupil. That's reliable without needing a texture, though I still need to figure out texture allocation across 5-12 textures total.

I'm considering placing a circular eye texture on a flat disc oriented along the outward normal, but that might clash visually with the bulging ellipsoid shape. Simpler approach: keep the glowing orange ball as the eyeball, then add a slit-textured circle plane offset outward from its surface by the ball's radius so it sits flush on top.

Checking the geometry math confirms the disc stays fully above the sphere surface at radius .04 with offset .046, giving a clean glowing slit-eye look against a dark orange socket. Now I'm working out the outward-facing direction and local position for placing the eye on the head.

Next I'm defining a helper to scale coordinate arrays by the head size, then laying out the jaw as a separate jointed part with its own frustum box and bone, plus chin spikes and teeth — placing upper fangs and lower tooth rows as spikes along the snout's bottom edge.

Setting up the jaw box geometry to overlap slightly with the upper teeth bed before posing it open, then placing upper and lower teeth along the mouth edges with larger fangs positioned toward the front.

Given the triangle budget, I'm keeping tooth geometry minimal with low side counts per spike so the full set across all heads stays well under the 60k triangle limit.

For horns, I'm sweeping a bezier curve from base to tip with a tapered radius profile, colored and parented to the head bone, using a low side count to keep polygon count cheap.

Also planning spikes down the back of the head and cheek frills as extruded fin-shaped plates, computing their orientation vectors from the head bone's local back/up directions.

Checking the frill polygon doesn't self-intersect, and it looks clean. Now I'm planning small dark nostril spheres near the snout tip, and considering how to add God of War-style battle scars—maybe as decal stripes or a texture on the skull rather than full geometry.

Scrapping the plane-based scar idea since it won't wrap well on a curved cranium; instead I'll use a procedural paint function with noise to give the hide a charred, ash-grey look with ember-orange cracks showing through thin spots, going for that Muspelheim aesthetic—colored but not emissive since paint can't glow. Settling on a draugr gray-green hide with bone armor plates, rust-iron fittings, and glowing ember-orange rune accents.

I'm finalizing the palette: dark green-grey hide, pale bone belly, blood-red mouth interior, iron fittings, and amber rune glow with fiery orange-yellow eyes. I'm also considering adding God of War details like broken iron shackles around a couple of the hydra's necks for extra brutal flavor.

Writing the rune collar geometry...

I like the idea of broken shackles instead of plain collars—each neck gets a rusted iron collar with a shattered chain hanging from it, built from small torus links dangling down the front of the neck from the collar's anchor point.

Actually chains on the neck might clip into the body, so I'll move them to the legs instead: shackle cuffs circling the front leg joints with broken chains trailing off, using a sweep around the leg radius plus some clearance for the cuff ring, with a few trailing torus links lying along the ground.

I should also add an embedded weapon for flavor — maybe a broken battle axe or spear haft stuck in the shoulder or back, built from a simple rod with an extruded blade and a rune detail.

I'm also planning an axe embedded in the flank with a glowing frost effect, working out the handle and axe-head placement using the embed and normal offset math so the geometry sinks correctly into the surface.

I realize typechecking might actually be enforced, so I need to be careful with TypeScript details—unused variables, implicit any, null checks on things like `around().at()` returning Hit or null—and avoid risky casts, only importing what's actually used. I should check what types are exported, like Joint, Frame, and Hit.

I'll rely on types like `Builder`, `Frame`, `Joint`, and `Part` since kit sources already use them, treating hits as Frame where Hit isn't clearly exported. Then I start planning the creature's body paint—dark green-grey scales with mottling and a pale belly.

Writing paint composition code...

I should double check that the SDK exports everything I need—cells, noise, mix, smoothstep, paint, scales, countershade—since the index likely re-exports the whole paint module. Now I'm thinking about adding armored dorsal plates running along the spine as a textural detail.

For the plates, I'm placing cone-shaped geometry along the body sweep using the spine's normal frames, flattening them into blade-like shapes with scale adjustments so they read as flat triangular plates rather than full cones, oriented so they thin out along the z-axis running down the spine.

I'm also considering adding shoulder pauldron-style bone armor plates for a more armored, creature-like silhouette.

For bone spurs, I'll scatter cone shapes across the body surface, filtering hits by normal direction to concentrate them on upper/forward-facing areas, colored in a horn-like tone.

Now planning the texture set: a glowing slit-eye SVG, a runic amber-on-dark glyph texture for collar studs, and a scar/war-paint decal with stitched sutures across the flank.

I'm deciding to use decal() to apply the rune ring emblem and scars directly onto the body surface, since decals accept any sweep target and can be layered with glow effects. For things like axe heads, I'll stick with paint-based rune stripes instead of textures since extrusions only support paints, not full textures — skipping fins, chains, wings, and teeth details as unnecessary, and considering a tattered cloth banner element.

I'm leaning toward adding small glowing ember cards scattered across the back and cracks instead of a full banner, giving a fiery Greek-myth feel without extra complexity, and I'm sketching out a texture list including the eye and rune ring sigils.

For the collar detail, I'll use rune plaques built from box geometry showing a full glyph on each face, with five distinct rune variants (one per head) generated through a small glyph-drawing function. That brings the texture count to nine total: eye, sigil, scar, flame, and five rune variants for the collar plaques.

For placement, I'm computing an outward-facing direction at each neck by subtracting the tangent's projection from a forward vector, then positioning the plaque at the collar surface along that direction using the collar radius plus a small offset.

Still writing plaque mesh...

I should now sketch the rest pose: heads fanned out, tail splayed, jaws open roughly 15–25°. For head detail counting I'm tallying components per head—skull, upper box, nose bump, eyes, brows, horns, nostrils, jaw, chin, cheek frills, teeth, and tongue—to make sure the part budget holds up across all heads.

I'll add a red mouth-interior box and a thin tongue piece, bringing total head parts to around 40, which scaled across heads plus the body lands near 300 parts total—comfortably within the 180–340 target. I'm also sanity-checking triangle counts per primitive type and confirming the scale-paint texture approach works consistently across all heads before moving on to leg details.

For the legs I'm planning shoulder spheres as bone pauldrons, heavy three-toed paws with claws and dew claws, and a six-joint tapering tail ending in a spiked bone club with dorsal spines running along its length. I'm also adding haunch ellipsoids at the hips and shoulders to bulk out the hind and fore leg bases before chaining in the joint hierarchy.

I'm nudging the belly position slightly lower for a heavier look, setting leg joint heights (hip around 1.45, foot near ground at 0.15), and noting the creature's overall scale—body roughly 2.5m with necks stretching heads up to around 4.2m. I'm working through the skeletal structure: how the sweep function maps radius along the chain's parametric t value, how the spine chain generates joints from its catmull-rom path spans, and confirming the hips joint placement aligns correctly with the first spine joint. I'm also setting up the tail chain to originate from the hips, and figuring out how to parent the neck bones to the last spine joint so the necks attach properly at the base.

Now I'm naming the neck and head joints based on left/right symmetry (center, L1/L2, R1/R2), and defining each neck chain as a sequence of four joints plus a head tip aimed along the path's end tangent.
